name: Chara
confidence_why: The only claim that Chara has stress is Aklilu Yilma's explicitly provisional one-sentence remark in a 12-page 1995 survey sketch (republished 2002), while the other fieldworker to describe the language, Mulugeta Seyoum (2018, 2023), labels the same kind of minimal-pair contrast tone without analysing it, and Dubale Sahile (2011) notes that the language's tone was never studied, so whether Chara's lexical contrast is stress or tone remains unanalysed.

catalog_locator: section 2.3 'Suprasegmental', p. 6 (p. 6); also section 2.2 'Vowels', p. 6 on [ä] in unstressed syllables
catalog_quote: 2.3 Suprasegmental. At the present state of my analysis, Chara seems to be a stress language. The following examples illustrate that stress is phonemic in the language. bakʼá 'empty' wóya 'to come' bákʼa 'to slap' woyá 'wolf'

audit.recode_to: Keep lexical (contrastive word prosody) but flag prosodic type as 'stress vs tone undetermined' and add a contra/caution entry citing Mulugeta Seyoum 2018: 5 and 2023: 53 (tone analysis: H vs L marks gender on object pronouns; geʃaˊ vs geʃa 'younger sister/brother' a tone difference). If the catalog separates tone languages from lexical-stress languages, this record is a candidate for moving to the tone/undetermined class pending Aklilu 1999.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim on printed/p. 6 of the held, section 2.3, and the [ä]-in-unstressed-syllables sentence is on the same page in 2.2, as the locator says. (2) The deciding source is a 12-page 1995 survey sketch (SIL republication 2002) whose prosody statement is a single explicitly provisional sentence with two disyllabic minimal pairs and no argument for stress over tone; the source is internally inconsistent on one of the two pairs (bäkʼá 'to slap' in 2.2 vs bákʼa 'to slap' in 2.3). Glottolog lists no reference grammar or phonology for Chara; the fuller Aklilu 1999 JELL paper (31-55) and Cerulli 1938 are print-only and not yet obtained. (3) Web search found and I downloaded the only recent first-hand descriptive work, Mulugeta Seyoum's SEL papers (2018, 2022, 2023) and Dubale Sahile's 2011 AAU MA thesis. sources.citation: Mulugeta Seyoum. 2023. Notes on Noun inflections in Tsaratsa. Studies in Ethiopian Languages 12: 47-58.
sources.quote: 'In my data the meaning difference is due to tone differences for instance, geʃaˊ 'younger sister' and geʃa 'younger brother'; ʔizi 'he' ʔi-s 'him' ... ʔiza 'she' ʔiˊ-s 'her' ʔiˊziri 'for her'.' Treats the suprasegmental contrast as tone, not stress; no general prosody section.
sources.note: Explicitly reanalyses an Aklilu 1995 minimal pair as a tone difference (p. 53).

sources.citation: Mulugeta Seyoum. 2018. Gender Marking in Tsaratsa. Studies in Ethiopian Languages 7: 1-13.
sources.quote: 'The subject pronouns are marking gender morphologically, while the object pronouns are marking with super segmental features, tone. ... ʔizi 'he' / ʔizí 'him'; ʔiza 'she' / ʔizi 'her' ... the objective personal pronoun has no morphological gender distinction but rather gender is distinct by tone. The masculine gender is marked by high tone while the feminine is marked by low tone.' Also p. 3-4: Tsegaye & Wubalem (2016) sketch grammar is '37 pages of rough description and 10 pages of word glosses' with 'a number of errors'.
sources.note: Most recent first-hand fieldwork description; states object pronouns distinguish gender by high vs low tone (p. 5) — bears directly on whether Aklilu's 'phonemic stress' pairs are tonal.

sources.citation: Mulugeta Seyoum. 2022. The Trilingual Vocabulary of Chara Language. Studies in Ethiopian Languages 11: 1-30 (Research Note).
sources.quote: No statement on stress or tone; c. 114 entries carry an unexplained acute/prime diacritic (e.g. yinzaˊ 'ancient', beˊseˊn 'accompany', munɗaʹ 'anus'), consistent with the author's tonal marking elsewhere but undefined here.
sources.locator: whole document (30 pp wordlist, no prose)

sources.citation: Dubale Sahile. 2011. Documentation and Description of Chara Verb Morphology. MA thesis, Addis Ababa University (62 pp). AAU-ETD handle 123456789/23726.
sources.quote: Phoneme charts adapted from Aklilu only; no suprasegmental section. Under limitations: 'It seems good if the study included all the language elements and the tone of the language.' — i.e. the author presumes tone but did not study it.
